The question

Can agreement between independent translators replace a gold formula?

Checking whether a first-order logic formula says what its sentence says usually needs a gold reference, and gold references are often wrong: one audit found errors in 39–42% of the annotations in two standard benchmarks. The paper tests a gold-free alternative. Ask translators from several independent LLM families to formalise the same sentence, check every pair for logical equivalence with the Z3 solver, and score each candidate by the share of peers that disagree with it. This is the .

On 221 templated sentences with exception clauses and a , the pre-registered test compares consensus with a cheap LLM judge by :

Consensus against the disguised flash-lite judge, recomputed in your browser from the rows both scored. The paper reports Δ = +0.367 [+0.328, +0.404], which passed the pre-registered criterion.

    Where it fails

    Three places the method breaks

    Which correct translations does consensus flag?

    Each template sentence has a of its exception clause, and both count as correct. When most families choose the weak reading, a correct translation of the strong one has few equivalent peers.

    What the paper does not show

    • Confirmation on fresh data is incomplete. A held-out set of 550 new sentences (E2-A) was built, but the run's budget ran out before enough items were labelled. On the one testable stratum (short ProverQA sentences) consensus ties a local Qwen-8B judge, Δ = +0.003 [−0.042, +0.052]. On 42 long L25 items (35 ERROR / 7 CORRECT, 3 sentences) c_score_align falls to 0.443, an estimate with extreme variance.
    • The 0.954 result is scoped to templates with a supplied signature. The signature removes the alignment problem entirely, which is why the AUROC is so high. It does not extend to translators that choose their own names.
    • Free-vocabulary out-of-sample labels are provisional. The gloss gate that would confirm MAPPED rows failed twice (balanced accuracy 0.776, then 0.561, against a 0.90 bar), so no row is a confirmed CORRECT. On a 146-row two-auditor subset the gain over the original-view judge is +0.105 [+0.011, +0.215].
    • Development labels come from a panel whose agreement is imperfect, and R_COMP-SIG later served as development data for aligner tuning, so the numbers on E are not independent of it.
    • Error typing does not work outside a shared vocabulary: 0.123 [0.081, 0.169] on E, below the judge (0.326) and the peer-medoid baseline (0.328).
    • Cost. With k = 9 families on R_COMP-SIG, the amortised consensus cost per candidate is about 19 times one cheap judge call.
    • Domain. English to FOL only, from MALLS, ProverQA and R_COMP. Other logics, languages and sentence distributions are untested.
